In summary, while it is apparent that the size of commercial zones may be a factor in plantsite location, the evidence submitted by the Little study shows a substantial diffusion of population and industrial activity away from the central city in spite of the present population-mileage formula. Furthermore, the surveys conducted by EDA reveal a wide range of factors which are deemed important location determinants, many of which have no direct relation to the commercial zone question. The absence of any specific data to support the proposition that there is a nexus between the size of commercial zones and land use patterns leads to the conclusion that expansion of the formula will not alter significantly current metropolitan land use patterns. State somewhat differently, it appears that the provision of motor carrier transportation service generally follows expanded commercial and industrial activity and is not the prime location determinant.
III. Adverse Effects Which Cannot Be Avoided
A motor carrier which operates wholly within a given commercial zone or terminal area is exempt from economic regulation. Consequently, the Commission does not regulate the number of carriers which are permitted to operate within these zones, nor does it examine the competitive effects of new exempt carrier operations. The commercial zone exemption reflects a policy judgment by Congress that motor carriers which conduct only local operations should be exempt from economic regulation. The primary rationale behind this policy is that motor carriers should be flexible enough to meet changing market conditions in urban areas. The purpose of this proceeding is not to change the basic thrust of the commercial zone and terminal area exemption, but rather to carry out the Congressional mandate by making commercial zones and terminal areas more reflective of current demographic and market conditions.
